A Bloemfontein based chartered accountant, Elrine Jacobs (41), was arrested on 20 November  2026 for allegedly using over R24 million of a non-profit company for online gambling. To enable the gambling spree, she is further alleged to have used the company Chief Executive Officer's electronic signature to fraudulently move money out of the company credit card. Thereafter, the accused presented false financial statements in order to cover her tracks. 

This was reported to Serious Commercial Crime Investigation Unit in Bloemfontein culminating in a warrant for her arrest being issued. 

Elrine Jacobs was granted bail of R50 000 and the matter postponed to 20 January 2027.

Each round got stricter, and the selling still hasn't stopped.

posts.text:
A lot here is worth thinking through.

1. Everyone agrees 2027 is going to be huge. The real uncertainty is 2028. Look at what Oracle and the Chinese hyperscalers are saying. A decline in capex in 2028 is becoming the consensus view.

2. Anthropic still hasn’t convinced investors it can hit $150B in ARR by the end of 2027. Most people see around $120B as more realistic.

3. If I had to buy a semiconductor stock right now, TSMC would be my only pick. It runs its business as conservatively as possible, even if that means losing orders to competitors. Remember that recent Taiwanese media report saying TSMC reviewed customers’ financial statements and required cash up front if they wanted to place additional orders. TSMC really is the Coca-Cola of SOXX.

4. Many market research firms and sell-side analysts expect memory prices to start falling in Q3 2027. If it starts to look like prices can avoid a collapse in the second half of 2027, I think memory stocks could rebound as early as Q1.

5. With Jensen gone, CPO is the most at risk. He was the only one pushing CPO despite low yields, and now even Nvidia seems to be leaning toward NPO. Long NPO, short CPO.

6. 3–5 GW of capacity in Southeast Asia? That’s more than I expected.

Thanks for sharing these great insights from China, @AgenticTeddy!

🇺🇸🇮🇷 The U.S. may have just fought a war that leaves Iran MORE powerful than before.

Thomas Friedman has returned from meetings with diplomats and analysts in Abu Dhabi with a deeply unsettling account of the mood in the Gulf.

Iran is reportedly disabling Emirati oil tankers with precision strikes, threatening regional infrastructure and demonstrating that it can disrupt energy supplies even while facing an American blockade.

And Gulf leaders are beginning to question whether Washington actually knows how to end this war.

I think the most disturbing possibility is that Iran doesn't need to defeat the U.S. military to emerge stronger.

It only needs to survive long enough to convince its neighbors that America cannot protect them from the consequences of confronting Tehran.

Friedman also describes a region increasingly splitting into competing alliances, with Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan pursuing their own diplomatic channels.

The U.S. has overwhelming military superiority. But Iran may be gaining something far more consequential: leverage over the countries that have to live next door to it.

And once those countries start doubting American security guarantees, rebuilding that trust could prove considerably harder than destroying another Iranian military installation.

Source: Thomas Friedman via the NYT / Writer: Oliver
